blocks.text: An electron microscope uses the wave nature of electrons, whose de Broglie wavelength can be thousands of times shorter than the wavelength of visible light. This lets it show fine details that an optical microscope cannot. Electrons from a source pass through an electromagnetic lens called the condenser, which focuses the beam on the specimen. The beam is accelerated by voltages that can reach megavolts; the higher the speed of the electrons, the shorter their wavelength and the higher the resolution. An electromagnetic objective lens forms an image of the specimen, which is further magnified by an electromagnetic projector lens and photographed; the photograph is called a micrograph (Fig 18.8).

Modern scanning electron microscopes can give three-dimensional images of remarkable quality. Electron microscopes can show details down to the nanometre scale, near the atomic level. They are used to study cell structure, viruses and bacteria in microbiology, to investigate fractures in metals, and to study materials and crystal structures.

blocks.alt: A vertical column with a dashed axis. Electrons from the electron source pass the magnetic condenser and converge on the specimen; the magnetic objective forms the first image, and the electromagnet image projector forms the second magnified image at the bottom.
